855.title: The Wartburg
855.hook: hidden in a castle, Luther translates the New Testament into everyday German
855.howItsDone: Christians across churches read the Bible in their own languages today, and Bible translators still face Luther's question of how close to stay to the original wording and how close to ordinary speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Worms: Luther before the emperor, his conscience captive to the word of God. Your line was here I stand.

A wagon on a forest road, heading home from Worms. Horsemen burst out of the trees, drag one passenger out, and gallop off with him. Word spreads that Luther has been seized, maybe killed. In fact the kidnapping is a rescue, arranged by his own prince to hide him. That night he's taken up to a castle on a hill, the Wartburg. His monk's habit is gone. He lets his hair and beard grow, and the castle staff call him Knight George. And there, an outlaw now, he picks up the Greek New Testament.

Luther worked from the Greek text Erasmus had printed, the one from a few days ago. He set out to put it into German: not German bent into the shape of the Latin, word for word, but German the way people actually spoke it. In a letter defending his translation, he explained how. You don't ask the Latin letters how to speak German, he wrote. You ask the mother in the house, the children in the street, the common man in the market, and you watch their mouths as they talk. Then you translate that way, and they'll understand you. He even gave an example. In the King James Bible, Jesus says: "for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." Put word for word into German, Luther said, that sounds like nobody's mother talking. A German mother would say something closer to: when the heart is full, the mouth runs over. So that's what he wrote. Not every scholar liked it. Some said he bent the text, and Luther pushed back hard. There's also an old story that he threw his inkwell at the devil in that room. It may well be a legend. What isn't legend is the result: a New Testament in German that could be read aloud at home, in the language of the market. And the work didn't belong only to Protestants. Catholic scholars produced German Bibles too, and in English, translators like Tyndale were doing the same thing, chasing the words of ordinary speech.

Choose one thing you know well that other people find confusing, your job, the rules of a game, a line of scripture, and explain it in your head in the words you'd use with a child at the kitchen table. If a word sounds like a document, swap it for one that sounds like a person, until the whole thing sounds like talk. If you pray, offer that plain explanation as a gift.
The Wartburg. The castle where Luther hid as Knight George and turned the Greek New Testament into the everyday German of the house, the street and the market.
Your line: the language of the market. Plain words can carry deep things. See you soon.

856.title: Katharina von Bora
856.hook: a nun who escaped, tradition says, in a herring cart, married Luther, and ran a brewery, farm and household
856.howItsDone: Lutheran churches remember Katharina von Bora, and some honor her in their calendars of commemoration; her household is often held up in Protestant teaching as a picture of the pastor's family and home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Wartburg: Luther in hiding as Knight George, translating for the market. Your line was the language of the market.

Behind a convent wall, in the days before Easter, a group of nuns have been reading pamphlets smuggled in from Wittenberg, and they've decided to leave. Leaving is dangerous. A merchant who brings goods to the convent agrees to help. One night his covered cart rolls away loaded with empty barrels, barrels that once held herring, tradition says. Tucked among them, hardly breathing, are the nuns. The cart makes it out. Among the women who climb down at the other end, smelling of fish, is Katharina von Bora.

Katharina had been placed in a convent as a girl. Now she was out, with no money and no family able to take her in, and the reformers tried to find husbands for the women who had left. For Katharina, a match was tried and fell through. Then, the story goes, she let it be known she would marry Luther, or one other man, and no one else. Luther was surprised, and then he did it. They moved into his old monastery building in Wittenberg, and she turned it into a household. She brewed beer. She kept a farm, cows and pigs, a garden, an orchard and a fishpond. She fed students who boarded with them, and refugees, and a stream of guests who came to argue theology at her table. She managed the money, which was not Luther's gift. She nursed the sick, and she raised their children. Luther's letters to her are full of teasing affection. He calls her my lord Katie, putting the word for a lord or master in front of her name. He calls her a rich woman, a doctor, a preacher, a brewer. In his will he left everything to her, which surprised people at the time. Proverbs has a poem for a woman like this, the capable wife. In the King James Bible: "She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness." Catholic and Lutheran readers tell her story differently. For Catholics, leaving a convent broke solemn vows. For the reformers, marriage was a holy calling too. Either way, a movement runs on someone who keeps the house standing.

Bring to mind one person whose work keeps your life running and mostly goes unseen: someone who cooks, schedules, cleans, remembers birthdays, pays the bills. Think of one specific thing they did this week. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if you don't, simply hold that one thing with gratitude.
Katharina. The nun who escaped in a wagon of barrels, married Luther, and ran the brewery, farm and household at the heart of the Wittenberg reform.
Your line: my lord katie. Luther's teasing names were love in plain words. Day eight hundred fifty-six, complete.

857.title: A mighty fortress
857.howItsDone: Lutheran churches sing "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God," and other churches sing it too; Psalm 46 is read in worship and in private prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katharina von Bora, who, tradition says, left her convent in a herring cart and ended up running Luther's household, farm and brewery. Your line was my lord katie.

"God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." That's how Psalm 46 opens in the King James Bible. Then look what it does next. The earth moves. The mountains slide into the sea. The waters roar. By its second verse the psalm is standing in the middle of the shaking, and it says, right there, we will not fear. Martin Luther turned this psalm into a hymn. In his German it opens Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott. In English it's often sung as a mighty fortress is our God.

The psalm is short and strange. Its second verse, in the King James wording: "Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed." Not because nothing bad is happening. Because God is a refuge while it happens. Then, in the middle of all that roaring water, a different water appears: "There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God." Floods outside, a gentle river inside the city. And near the end, after bows broken and spears cut in two, comes this: "Be still, and know that I am God." It comes right after talk of war, not at a spa. Luther took the psalm's refuge and made it a castle, a fortress with walls. His verses name an old enemy, the devil, scheming and armed. They admit human strength won't win that fight, and they name the one who fights for us: Christ. A single little word, the hymn says, can bring the enemy down. The last verse is the bravest. In paraphrase: let them take our goods, our honor, even our families and our lives; they gain nothing, and the kingdom still stands. So one psalm gives two pictures: a fortress to shelter in when the enemy comes, and a river and a stillness in the middle of the city. Some Christians lean on the walls, some on the stillness. The psalm holds both.
screen: `A RIVER IN THE CITY OF GOD.`
`BE STILL, IN THE MIDDLE OF A WAR.`

If reading isn't possible right now, hold its three pictures instead: mountains sliding into the sea, a river running quietly through a city, and the words be still. If you pray, let the first verse be your prayer; if you don't, sit with whichever picture keeps coming back.

858.title: The small catechism
858.hook: Luther wrote a simple Q&A for families: what does this mean?
858.howItsDone: Lutheran churches use Luther's Small Catechism to teach children and adults, especially before confirmation; Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed churches teach with catechisms of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Burg: Psalm 46 and the fortress hymn Luther built on it. Your line was a river, and a stillness.

A small booklet, open on a table at home. A parent reads a line out loud: "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." Then comes the question the booklet asks after almost every line: what does this mean? And a child answers, in a sentence short enough to remember. That's the scene Martin Luther wrote for. In the preface to his Small Catechism, he describes going around the parishes and being shocked at what he found: ordinary people who barely knew the Lord's Prayer or the commandments, and pastors who couldn't teach them. His answer wasn't a thicker book. It was a thinner one.
screen: `A BOOKLET ON THE TABLE AT HOME.`
`NOT A THICKER BOOK. A THINNER ONE.`

segments.voice: A catechism is a teaching book, usually in questions and answers, for learning the basics of the faith. Luther also wrote a larger one for pastors. The small one has a note at the top of each part: this is how the head of a household should teach it, simply, to the family. So the classroom he had in mind was a home. It walks through the Ten Commandments, the Apostles' Creed and the Lord's Prayer, then baptism, confession and the Lord's Supper. After each piece comes the same short question: what does this mean? The answers are plain. The first commandment, no other gods: in Luther's answer, we should fear, love and trust God above all things. One breath. Or take the Lord's Prayer: "Give us this day our daily bread." What does daily bread mean? Luther's answer sounds like a household inventory. It includes food and drink, clothing and shoes, house and home, fields and cattle, money and goods, a faithful spouse, good government, good weather, peace, health, good friends and faithful neighbors, and the like. Shoes and good weather, inside the Lord's Prayer. The question does something on its own, too. It assumes words you've said over and over might still be closed to you, and it invites you to open them. Lutheran churches still teach with it. Catholic, Orthodox and Reformed Christians have catechisms of their own, each with its own questions and answers. But Luther's small question is one anyone can borrow.

Choose one line you've said so often it slides past: a line of the Lord's Prayer, a blessing before meals, a saying a grandparent used to repeat. Say it once, slowly, then ask the catechism's question and answer it in one plain sentence of your own. If you pray, end by saying the line again as a prayer; if not, let your sentence sit.
Catechism. A teaching book of questions and answers on the basics of the faith. Luther's small one was written to be taught at home.

859.title: Zwingli's sausages
859.hook: in Zurich, eating sausages in Lent starts a reformation
859.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep set fasts in Lent, such as abstaining from meat on certain days; some Protestant Christians fast or give something up by personal choice during Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luther's Small Catechism, a thin book for teaching at home, and its one question. Your line was what does this mean?

The presses at a Zurich print shop have been running hard. The printer, Christoph Froschauer, has a big job due, and his workers are worn out. It's Lent, the season before Easter, when the church of their day forbids meat. At a meal in the printer's house, the story goes, someone brings out sausages, cut up and shared around the table. A local priest is in the room: Huldrych Zwingli. Word gets out, the city council gets involved, and a plate of sausages turns into a public question about the whole church.

Here's the odd part. By the usual account, Zwingli didn't eat any. He sat at the table and let it happen. But when the eaters were accused, he stood up for them, in a sermon later printed as On the Choice and Freedom of Foods. His argument went to the Bible: where does scripture command this? He pointed to Paul, in the King James Bible: "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday." Fasting, Zwingli said, can be a good thing, and anyone who wants to fast in Lent should be free to. But it shouldn't be a law that binds every conscience under threat of punishment. That's the hinge: not a rule against fasting, but a question about who gets to make the rule. Once Zurich asked that about sausages, it asked it about everything else, until the city's church was reshaped around preaching from scripture. Paul has a second line that cuts both ways: "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth." The eater shouldn't sneer. The faster shouldn't judge. Christians keep Lent in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep the Lenten fast together, as a discipline of the whole church. Some Protestant Christians fast by choice, or give something up. Underneath it all is Zwingli's honest question: why do we do this?
screen: `LET NO MAN JUDGE YOU IN MEAT.`

segments.voice: Think of one rule you keep without thinking: a religious habit, a family custom, the way things are always done at work. Ask Zwingli's question gently, why do we do this, and look for the reason; sometimes there's a good one, and sometimes it's just habit. If you pray, ask for wisdom about it; if you don't, hold the rule up to the light for a while.
Zwingli's sausages. A meal in Lent in a Zurich print shop that Zwingli defended, and a question about rules that reshaped a city's church.
Your line: why do we do this? One honest question reshaped a whole city's church. See you tomorrow.

860.title: Felix Manz (1527)
860.hook: baptized as adults, an early Anabaptist martyr is drowned by other Protestants
860.howItsDone: Mennonite, Amish, Hutterite and other Anabaptist-descended churches baptize those who confess faith for themselves and remember their early martyrs, including Felix Manz, and nonviolence is part of their heritage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zwingli's sausages, and a question about rules that spread through Zurich. Your line was why do we do this?

A small boat pushes out into the river that runs through Zurich. In it is a young man with his hands bound: Felix Manz. He had studied with Zwingli, read the Bible with him, cheered the questions Zwingli raised. And he took those questions one step further than the city would allow. Now the city council of Zurich, a Protestant council in a Protestant city, has sentenced him to be drowned. The accounts say he sang as they took him out. Today's word is the name opponents gave him and his friends: Anabaptist.
screen: `A BOAT ON THE RIVER IN ZURICH.`

segments.voice: Here's the step. Manz and a circle of friends, Conrad Grebel among them, read the New Testament and noticed that baptisms there follow faith. People hear, believe, then are baptized. So shouldn't baptism come after a person can confess faith for themselves? They began baptizing one another as adults, in a house in Zurich. Opponents called them Anabaptists, re-baptizers, since they'd been baptized as infants. They didn't accept the name; to them, this was their first real baptism. The council outlawed it. Manz was arrested, released, arrested again, and finally drowned in the river. Christians still answer the baptism question differently, and both answers have deep roots. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches baptize infants, seeing baptism as God's gift and promise, given before a child can ask. Mennonites, Baptists and others baptize those who confess faith themselves. Manz's circle held something else too. They refused to take up the sword, even to defend themselves, and early Anabaptist confessions said so plainly. Their picture came from Isaiah, who sees a world where, in the King James words, "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb," and "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain." The peaceable kingdom. It's hard to sit with. In those years, Christians put other Christians to death over how and when to baptize. Manz was killed by a city whose reformers had once read the Bible beside him, and he went to the river still believing Jesus' followers should never hurt anyone.
screen: `THE WOLF SHALL DWELL WITH THE LAMB.`

segments.voice: Start with Felix Manz in the boat, then widen it: Anabaptists, Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox Christians, who in more than one place and time have suffered at the hands of other Christians, and some still do. Hold them in mind without needing to decide who was most to blame. If you pray, pray for them and for those who hurt them; if you don't, keep them company in silence.

861.title: Menno Simons
861.hook: a Dutch priest who joined the Anabaptists and gave the Mennonites his name
861.howItsDone: Mennonite churches, named after Menno Simons, baptize believers, practice nonviolence and simple living, and are known for relief work such as sharing food, clothing and shelter.

segments.voice: Last time: Felix Manz, drowned in Zurich, and the name Anabaptist. Your line was the peaceable kingdom.

A village priest in Friesland, in the north of the Netherlands, is saying Mass. He holds up the bread, and a doubt he can't shake rises with it. He keeps his post and his comfortable life. He reads the New Testament on the side, and the doubts grow. Then news comes that a group of Anabaptists has been killed, and tradition says his own brother was among them. Men who died for what they believed, he writes, while he stayed safe and said nothing. That thought won't leave him alone. His name is Menno Simons, and a whole family of churches still carries it.

Menno left the priesthood and joined the scattered, hunted Anabaptists of the Low Countries. He didn't start their movement; he came into it and became one of its shepherds. And he chose its peaceful side. Some who carried the Anabaptist name had turned to violence. Menno taught that Christ's followers do not take up the sword at all. From then on he lived on the move with his family, writing, preaching and baptizing believers, with authorities hunting him. His writings carried a verse from Paul, in the King James wording: "For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ." Everything had to stand on that. Those who followed his teaching came to be called Mennonites, after him. Then there's the passage his line comes from. In paraphrase, Menno wrote that true evangelical faith cannot lie dormant. It clothes the naked. It feeds the hungry. It comforts the sorrowful. It shelters the destitute. It serves even those who harm it. It binds up what is wounded. Faith, for Menno, gets up and does things. That fits the letter of James: "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone." Lutheran, Catholic, Reformed and Mennonite teachers put faith and works together in different ways. But Menno's list is about bread and blankets, and it came from a man who spent years with nowhere safe to sleep.

Look honestly at the day ahead and find one thing you could do without: a purchase you don't need, a second helping, an hour of scrolling. Then pick one thing from Menno's list to put in its place, clothes set aside to give, food for someone hungry, a word for someone sad. If you pray, offer that small trade to God; if you don't, hold the choice quietly and let it settle.
Menno Simons. A Dutch priest who joined the peaceful Anabaptists and became a leader of the churches now called Mennonite.
Your line: true faith cannot lie dormant. It gets up, and it feeds and clothes. That's day eight hundred sixty-one.
